package.title: The Hidden Fed Metric Breaking the Economy
package.promised: An explanation of a little-known Federal Reserve metric, why it is distorting policy or decision-making, and how that damage is spreading through the economy. I expect to leave knowing what the metric is, why it matters, and what consequences to watch for.

new_things: The Fed’s balance sheet fell by trillions while bank reserves barely changed.
Money market funds had parked about $2.5 trillion at the Fed.
By September 18, that pool of parked money was almost empty.
Companies are facing a debt wall.

new_things: More than $3 trillion in U.S. corporate debt matures from 2025 through 2027.
Replacing a 2% loan with a 7% loan would more than triple the interest cost.

new_things: Refinancing a 2% loan at 7% more than triples the interest bill even without taking on more debt.
The higher interest cost leaves less money for wages, materials, and hiring.

reports.held_question: How does the Federal Reserve support the financial system?

new_things: Stable bank balances can conceal that the banks’ financial buffer is shrinking.
Companies replacing cheap debt still need financing while a source of support behind banks is declining.
The video will trace where that support went.
reports.held_question: What is the support behind the banks, where did it go, and what happens as it runs down?

new_things: Money funds can leave cash at the Federal Reserve overnight and earn a return.
Treasury securities back that transaction.
The Fed calls the arrangement overnight reverse repo.
Money funds can also earn money elsewhere.
reports.held_question: Where else can money funds earn money, and what happens when they move cash there?

new_things: Money funds can also buy Treasury bills or lend in private markets.
When those alternatives pay better, money funds can withdraw cash from the Fed.
Those withdrawals helped banks hold steady while the Fed reduced its own investments.
reports.held_question: How did money funds withdrawing cash from the Fed help banks hold their ground?

new_things: The Fed owns Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities.
Quantitative tightening is when the Fed lets those investments mature without fully replacing them, causing its assets to fall.
reports.held_question: Why did money funds withdrawing cash from the Fed help banks hold their ground during quantitative tightening?

new_things: A shrinking Fed balance sheet would normally mean banks have less cash.
At the same time, money-market funds were reducing their balances in the Fed's overnight reverse-repo facility.
The simplified example starts with the Fed's assets falling by $100 billion.
reports.held_question: How does the drop in overnight reverse-repo balances offset the Fed's $100 billion asset reduction and affect bank cash?

new_things: In the example, the Fed’s reverse-repo balance falls by $100 billion.
The Fed owns $100 billion less and owes money funds $100 billion less.
Because the asset and reverse-repo balances fall together, banks’ Fed-account balances can stay unchanged.
reports.held_question: What happens to bank reserves when the reverse-repo balance can no longer offset the Fed’s shrinking assets?

new_things: Banks avoid losing cash when the Fed’s overnight reverse-repo account shrinks enough to offset the balance-sheet runoff.
The Fed’s June 2025 report compares account balances with their levels when runoff began in June 2022.
reports.held_question: How large were the offsetting movements shown in the Fed’s report?

new_things: From June 2022 to June 2025, the Fed’s assets fell by about $2.2 trillion.
Reverse repos outside the foreign-official accounts fell by about $1.8 trillion over that period.
Banks’ balances at the Fed rose by only $72 billion over that period.
reports.held_question: What happened to the government’s balance over that period?

new_things: The government’s cash account also fell, which helped offset the drain on banks.
Banks ended the period roughly holding their ground rather than gaining trillions in their Fed accounts.
Trillions withdrawn from other accounts mainly prevented banks’ balances from shrinking.
reports.held_question: What does the workshop’s machine still need?

new_things: A workshop still needs financing even if the bank providing it looks stable.
Stable bank balances can depend on support from other accounts.
Money funds cannot withdraw the same parked dollar twice.
reports.held_question: What had happened by September 18?

new_things: By September 18, 2026, money funds’ overnight balance was about half a billion dollars.
That account no longer has enough cash to provide another trillion-dollar offset.
Banks can appear steady even as a source of protection is being depleted.

new_things: The business must find the extra money for the higher interest cost.

Postponing the expansion would cost the equipment supplier a sale.

new_things: Delaying the expansion also delays hiring the person who would operate the new machine.
A business financing problem can affect people who never follow Federal Reserve charts.
An old fixed-rate loan protects a business from higher rates only until its renewal date.

new_things: The Fed found that new borrowing costs rose much faster than the cost of existing debt.
An existing cheap loan contract only delays the larger bill; it does not ensure the next contract will also be cheap.

new_things: A tax payment can reveal cash movement that a bank’s headline balance misses.
When you pay a tax bill, your bank reduces your deposit.
The bank settles the tax payment through the government’s checking account at the Federal Reserve.

new_things: The government’s balance rises by the amount of the tax payment.
The bank ends up with less money at the Fed.
The government’s checking account at the Fed is called the Treasury General Account.

new_things: A chart of the Fed’s assets would not show money leaving a bank’s account at the Fed.
When the government pays a contractor, money leaves the government’s account and goes to the contractor’s bank.
The contractor’s bank credits the contractor’s deposit.
reports.held_question: Does the contractor’s bank also gain the same amount in its account at the Fed?

new_things: The contractor payment moves cash back toward the banks.
Tax and government payments can change who holds money at the Fed without changing the Fed’s assets.
A useful first check is to identify which account changed.
The Fed publishes these account balances in its weekly balance-sheet release.
reports.held_question: What should I start with in the Fed’s weekly balance-sheet release?

new_things: To interpret a balance-sheet move, first identify the account and the dates being compared.
A decline in bank reserves is not the same kind of event as money-market funds withdrawing from the Fed’s overnight account.
A tax payment moves cash differently from the Fed allowing a security to mature.

new_things: There is an unofficial shortcut called net liquidity.
The net-liquidity formula starts with the Fed’s assets, then subtracts the government’s cash account and money funds’ overnight balance.
The shortcut can be useful.
reports.held_question: What can the net-liquidity shortcut help explain, and what does it miss?

new_things: The net-liquidity shortcut organizes the accounts but is neither an official Fed series nor a measure of bank reserves.
In the hundred-billion-dollar example, the two declines cancel because of how the subtraction works.
